openingMessage: Set your house in perfect order before you criticize the world.
openingWhy: Before we critique the operator's plan at the pre-job, the honest question: is our own trailer inspected, our bottles full, our forms real? On location, the crew whose house is in order is the crew that gets listened to when it counts.
leadershipThought: Nobody protects a location alone. The willingness to carry extra weight, communicate early, and check on the person next to you — that is coaching in action.

specialFocus.title: Recognition for Excellence
specialFocus.why: This week we handed out the first monthly awards — a backpack, a duck, and an attitude award — and every one of them was earned on paper anyone can check. That's the point of this morning: excellence at Canon isn't a feeling, it's visible. Michael Jobe just put up a perfect month — 61 audited checks, zero misses. Ralph Forbes went the whole month without a single auditor note. Pablo Soto ran 10 jobs and turned in 10 complete packets. None of them did it for a prize — but every one of them deserves to hear their name said out loud. Recognition is a leadership skill, not a mood: catch people doing it RIGHT, name the exact behavior, and do it in front of the crew. What gets recognized gets repeated — and what gets repeated becomes who we are.
specialFocus.standardLabel: How We Recognize — Make It Specific, Make It Loud
standard: Name the PERSON and the BEHAVIOR, not just 'good job.' 'Pablo turned in ten complete packets in ten jobs' teaches the whole circle what right looks like. 'Good job Pablo' teaches nothing.
Recognize the catch, not just the save. A duck — seeing a hazard and saying it out loud — is the everyday excellence that prevents the big day. Eagles get the headlines; ducks keep us alive.
Recognize in the moment, on location. If you see a tech do it right — a clean trailer flip, a sharp JSA, a stop-and-ask — say it there, then bring it to the morning meeting so everyone hears it.

Put it on paper. Write the OWL form about what went RIGHT — positive catches belong in the record just like hazards do. That's how names reach the Duck & Eagle board without a lead having to remember.
Spread it around. Excellence lives in the whole crew, not the same three names — if the same people get every mention, start looking harder at everyone else.
Leads: recognition is part of your job, not extra credit. One named, specific recognition from you this morning — pick someone whose work this week deserves the circle's attention.

scenarios.title: The Quiet Perfect Month
scenarios.body: Michael Jobe ran 31 shifts in September. Matt's audit checked his paperwork 61 times and found zero misses — the only note all month was one missing wellhead photo. Nobody saw him do anything dramatic. No stop-work, no save, no story. Just every form, every day, done right, when nobody was watching. Question for the circle: if we only recognize the dramatic saves, what are we telling the tech who's quietly perfect? Say his name this morning. That consistency IS the excellence.

scenarios.title: The Catch That Didn't Make the News
scenarios.body: A tech walks a location, notices a monitor mounted on a light plant, and says so — it gets moved to a stand before nightfall. No alarm, no incident, no report beyond a line on a form. That's a duck: seen, said, fixed. Multiply that by a crew that knows catches get NAMED at the morning meeting, and you get a location where problems get said out loud while they're still small. Recognition isn't the reward for the catch — it's the fuel for the next one.

questions: Who on your crew did something this week that deserves their name said in this circle — and what exactly did they do?
When's the last time you wrote someone ELSE's good catch on your own OWL form? Why don't we do that more?
What's the difference between 'good job' and recognition that actually changes behavior?
Who's the quietly consistent tech on your crew that never gets mentioned because they never make noise?
specialFocus.nonNegotiable: Every lead names one person and one specific behavior this morning — out loud, in the circle. Recognition that names a behavior is recognition that repeats it.
